blurb: A slow, long-lived Plant Select native from the Colorado Plateau: tight clusters of sapphire-blue stars in spring over narrow foliage that turns a clean, clear yellow in autumn. One of the few xeric perennials that gives real fall colour.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
spread: Compact and clumping; slow-growing, does not spread
seasons: Sapphire-blue star flowers April–June; foliage turns clear yellow in fall; dies back in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 7,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a. Plant Select rates it USDA zones 4–9 and grows it to about 6,200 ft on the Front Range.[1][3]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Clay, loam or sandy soils all suit it, which is unusual for a Colorado Plateau native; what it wants is drainage rather than a particular texture.[1][3]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 12–16 in wide. Clusters of star-shaped flowers over narrow leaves, with clear-yellow fall colour — a Plant Select® introduction.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from spring into midsummer; CSU records the colour as blue and the height as 10–14 in tall.[1][3]
care.maintenance: It is slow-growing, so Plant Select's advice is to start with larger nursery stock rather than a plug, and to make sure you are buying the true dwarf species and not *A. hubrichtii*, which reaches 3 ft in both directions.[1][3]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

Plant Select — Amsonia jonesii (Colorado desert blue star)

edible.summary: Not a food plant. It is a dogbane-family species with milky sap — treat the whole plant as inedible.[1][3]
edible.caution: No documented food use, and this guide classes it as not to be eaten. Plant Select notes that as a member of Apocynaceae (the dogbane family) it produces the milky sap characteristic of that family. Dogbane-family sap is characteristically irritant and the family contains genuinely poisonous plants, so keep the sap off skin and out of eyes when cutting it back, wash your hands afterwards, and don't let children or pets chew it. Don't reason across from the edible plants elsewhere in this guide.[1][3]
